rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs file system is a compressed read-only file system embedded in systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem type is a free version of the Veritas filesystem. It is the primary filesystem type for HP-UX operating systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs file system type is a hierarchical file system that allows Mac OS file systems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem designed to replace hfs, allowing Mac OS filesystems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 filesystem type (Journaling Flash File System 2) is a journaling filesystem used on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: Unused kernel filesystem modules are not available
rules.explanation: Unused file system modules (squashfs, udf, overlay) should not be loaded by the kernel on AKS nodes.
rules.impact: Unnecessary file system types increase the attack surface; overlay is especially sensitive in container environments.

rules.title: /tmp is mounted as a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is used for temporary files; on Kubernetes nodes a separate /tmp partition simplifies isolation.
rules.impact: Creating /tmp as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, making /tmp useless for an attacker to install executable code. It will also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/fstab or in systemd unit file tmp.mount

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is mounted as a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is a world-writable directory that can function as shared memory, facilitating inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Creating /dev/shm as its own file system allows an administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, making /dev/shm useless for an attacker placing executable code. It would also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /dev/shm file system is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create special devices on /dev/shm partitions.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the filesystem prevents users from introducing privileged programs into the system and having them executed by non-root users.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM package manager implements GPG key signing to verify package integrity during and after installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that updates are obtained from a valid source to protect against spoofing, which could result in the unintentional installation of malware on the system. To do this, ensure that GPG keys are configured correctly for your system.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/yum.repos.d/*, /etc/dnf/dnf.conf; GPG keys in /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/

rules.title: Gpgcheck is configured
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck option controls package signature verification after download.
rules.impact: It is important to always verify the RPM package signature before installation to ensure that the software was obtained from a trusted source.

rules.title: TDNF gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: TDNF is the Azure Linux (Mariner) package manager. The gpgcheck parameter in /etc/tdnf/tdnf.conf and in /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo.
rules.impact: Without RPM signature verification, substituted packages may be installed.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems must have the appropriate package manager repositories configured so that the system can receive the latest patches and updates.
rules.impact: If the system's package repositories are configured incorrectly, important patches may not be identified, or a rogue repository may introduce compromised software.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit-mitigation technique that randomly distributes the address space of key process data areas.
rules.impact: Random placement of virtual memory regions will make it more difficult to write exploits against memory pages, because memory placement will constantly change.

rules.title: Kernel dump backtracing is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program terminated abnormally. It can also be used to obtain sensitive information from a core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken at the moment the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is typically useful only to developers attempting to troubleshoot issues, increasing risk to the system.

rules.title: Kernel dump storage is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program terminated abnormally. It can also be used to obtain sensitive information from a core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image captured when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is typically useful only to developers attempting to debug issues.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password will require anyone rebooting the system to enter a password before they can set boot command-line parameters.
rules.impact: Requiring a boot password when the bootloader starts prevents an unauthorized user from entering boot parameters or modifying the boot partition. This prevents users from weakening security (for example, disabling SELinux at boot).
rules.scope: Settings in file user.cfg in directory /boot/grub2/

rules.title: Bootloader configuration access is configured
rules.explanation: Grub files contain boot configuration information and passwords used to unlock boot options.
rules.impact: Setting read and write permissions for root only prevents non-root users from viewing or modifying boot parameters. Non-root users who read boot parameters may identify security weaknesses at boot and exploit them.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and act as a message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: - IF - /etc/motd is not configured with correct access, it can be modified by unauthorized users using incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on at local terminals.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue.net file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Time synchronization is used
rules.explanation: System time must be synchronized (chrony) for accurate log timestamps and Kerberos.
rules.impact: Time desynchronization hinders incident investigation and breaks time-bound authentication.

rules.title: Chrony is configured with trusted NTP sources
rules.explanation: The server/pool directives in /etc/chrony.conf and /etc/chrony.d/*.conf specify time sources for the host.
rules.impact: Without configured time sources, an AKS node may drift relative to the cluster.

rules.title: Xinetd is not installed
rules.explanation: xinetd is a legacy network super-server; it is not used on AKS Optimized Azure Linux.
rules.impact: Legacy super-servers expand the attack surface.

rules.title: Xorg-x11-server-common is not installed
rules.explanation: The xorg-x11-server-common package contains X11 components that are not required on AKS server nodes.
rules.impact: The graphical stack increases the attack surface on hosts without a GUI.

rules.title: Avahi is not installed or not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi implements mDNS/DNS-SD for automatic service discovery on the local network.
rules.impact: Discovery services are not needed on cluster nodes and increase the attack surface.
rules.scope: avahi package, avahi-daemon.socket and avahi-daemon.service services

rules.title: The print server is not installed
rules.explanation: CUPS is a printing system that is not required on AKS Optimized Azure Linux nodes.
rules.impact: Unnecessary network services increase the attack surface.
rules.scope: cups package, cups.socket and cups.service services

rules.title: The DHCP server is not installed
rules.explanation: A DHCP server (kea and others) is not required on Kubernetes worker nodes.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically configured to operate as a DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the dhcp-server package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The DNS server is not installed
rules.explanation: The DNS server (bind/named) must not run on AKS nodes unless the node is a DNS server.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended to operate as a DNS server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The FTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: The FTP client transfers data without encryption; SFTP/SCP should be used for file transfer.
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or authentication credentials. If file transfer is required, it is recommended to use SFTP. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The FTP server is not installed
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The tftp server is not installed
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a TFTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to gain access to files.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The web server is not installed
rules.explanation: Web servers provide the ability to host website content.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a web server, it is recommended that the packages be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. Note: There are several HTTP servers. They should also be reviewed and removed if not needed.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The IMAP and POP3 server is not installed
rules.explanation: dovecot is an open-source IMAP and POP3 server for Linux-based systems.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. Note: There are several IMAP/POP3 servers that may use other service names. Those should also be reviewed and the packages removed if they are not required.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: Samba is not installed
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share file systems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise file systems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and file systems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this package can be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The HTTP proxy server is not installed
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically configured to operate as a proxy server, it is recommended that the squid package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. Note: There are several HTTP proxy servers. They should be reviewed and removed if not needed.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: Net-snmp is not installed or the snmpd service is not enabled
rules.explanation: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is a widely used protocol for monitoring the status and health of network equipment, computer hardware, and devices such as UPS units. Net-SNMP is a suite of applications used to implement SNMPv1 (RFC 1157), SNMPv2 (RFC 1901–1908), and SNMPv3 (RFC 3411–3418) over both IPv4 and IPv6. Support for classic SNMPv2 (also known as "historic SNMPv2" — RFC 1441–1452) was discontinued in version 4.0 of the UCD-snmp package. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP commands from an SNMP management system, execute commands or collect information, and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: The SNMP server can communicate using SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and does not require authentication to execute commands. SNMPv3 replaces the simple/cleartext password exchange used in SNMPv2 with more securely encoded parameters. If the SNMP service is not required, the net-snmp package should be removed to reduce the system's attack surface. Note: If a required dependency exists for the net-snmp package but the snmpd service is not required, that service should be masked. Note: If SNMP is required: • The server should be configured for SNMP v3 only. User authentication and message encryption must be configured. • If SNMP v2 is absolutely necessary, change the community string values.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The NIS server is not installed
rules.explanation: The ypserv package provides the Network Information Service (NIS). This service, officially known as "Yellow Pages", is a client-server directory service protocol for distributing system configuration files. An NIS server is a set of programs that enable configuration files to be distributed.
rules.impact: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks and buffer overflows and has weak authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has generally been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended to remove the ypserv package and use a more secure service if needed.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The telnet server is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow a user who can monitor network traffic to steal credentials. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and a higher level of security.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs), such as sendmail and Postfix, are used to listen for incoming mail and deliver messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If the system is not intended to operate as a mail server, it is recommended to configure the MTA to process local mail only.
rules.impact: Mail transfer agent software is complex, and most MTAs have a long history of security issues. Although it is important to ensure that the system can handle local mail messages, there is no need for the MTA daemon to listen on a port unless the server is intended to operate as a mail server that receives and processes mail from other systems. Note: • This recommendation is designed for the postfix mail server. • Depending on your environment, you may have an alternative MTA installed, such as sendmail. In that case, refer to the documentation of the installed MTA to configure the recommended state.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: Nfs-utils is not installed or the nfs-server service is masked
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most widely used file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides systems the ability to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not require shared network resources, it is recommended to remove the nfs-utils package to reduce the system's attack surface.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: Rsync-daemon is not installed or the rsyncd service is masked
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service can be used to synchronize files between systems over the network.
rules.impact: If it is not required, the rsync-daemon package should be removed to reduce the system's attack surface. The rsyncd service presents a security threat because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication. Note: If a required dependency exists for the rsync-daemon package but the rsyncd service is not required, this service should be masked.
rules.scope: Installed RPM packages and systemd services

rules.title: Time synchronization is used
rules.explanation: System time should be synchronized across all systems in the environment. This is typically done by establishing an authoritative time server or set of servers and synchronizing all system clocks to them.
rules.impact: Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos, and also ensures that log files have consistent timestamps across the enterprise, which aids forensic investigations.

rules.title: Chrony is configured
rules.explanation: The server directive specifies an NTP server that can be used as a time source. The pool directive is used to specify a pool of NTP servers rather than a single NTP server.
rules.impact: Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms and to ensure consistent timestamps in log files across the enterprise to assist forensic investigations.

rules.title: Chrony is not running as the root user
rules.explanation: The /etc/sysconfig/chronyd file allows configuration of chrony parameters, including the user under which chrony is started. By default the chrony user is used.
rules.impact: Services must not run as the root user.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and increased security and is included in most Linux distributions.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed
rules.explanation: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a method of looking up information in a central database.
rules.impact: If the system will not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended to remove the software to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The TFTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: The IPv6 status is defined
rules.explanation: IPv6 is based on 128-bit addressing and can support 340 undecillion unique addresses.
rules.impact: It is recommended to enable and configure IPv6 unless this conflicts with local site policy.
rules.scope: Parameters: ipv6 module state and disable_ipv6 sysctl parameters

rules.title: Wireless interfaces are not available
rules.explanation: Wireless networking is used when wired networks are unavailable.
rules.impact: If wireless communication is not to be used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf for wireless modules

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless communication technology used to exchange data between devices over short distances.
rules.impact: An attacker may find a way to access or damage your data. In addition, viruses or other malicious code may use Bluetooth technology to infect other devices.
rules.scope: Settings: bluez package installation, bluetooth.service status

rules.title: Icmp redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and instruct your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This mechanism allows an external routing device to update your system's routing tables.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This is a way to allow an external routing device to update your system's routing tables. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects, net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects, net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept any ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except they originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are most likely safe.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table updates from possibly compromised known gateways.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 forces the Linux kernel to use reverse path filtering for a received packet to determine whether the packet is valid. Essentially, with reverse path filtering, if the return packet does not leave from the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 is a good way to prevent attackers from sending your system spoofed packets that cannot be answered. One case where this feature does not work is when asymmetric routing is used. This can occur when using dynamic routing protocols (bgp, ospf, and so on) on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: On a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. In contrast, non-source-routed packets follow a path determined by routers in the network. In some cases systems may be unreachable or inaccessible from some locations (for example, private addresses or Internet-routable), so source-routed packets will need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route, net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route, net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system from accepting source-routed packets. Assume that this system is capable of routing packets to Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another interface. Assume that the private addresses do not support routing to Internet-routable addresses and vice versa. Under normal routing circumstances, an attacker using Internet-routable addresses cannot use the system as a means of accessing private-address systems. However, if source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to private-address systems because the route could be specified rather than relying on routing protocols that would not permit such routing.

rules.title: Logging of suspicious packets
rules.explanation: If this feature is enabled, packets with non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians and net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians to 1 enables this feature. Logging these packets allows the administrator to investigate the possibility that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system.

rules.title: TCP syncookies are enabled
rules.explanation: If tcp_syncookies is set, the kernel will process TCP SYN packets normally until the half-open connection queue fills, after which SYN cookie functionality takes effect. SYN cookies work by not using the SYN queue at all. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN/ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses, as well as the port number and the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to allow the connection even if there is no corresponding SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN flood attacks to deny service to the targeted system by sending many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This rapidly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents successful connections. Setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 1 enables SYN cookies, allowing the system to continue accepting valid connections even when a denial-of-service attack is occurring.

rules.title: Ipv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send Router Advertisement messages to announce their availability and convey information to neighboring nodes, allowing them to autoconfigure on the network. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra determine the system's ability to accept these advertisements.
rules.impact: It is recommended that systems not accept router advertisements, because they can be tricked into redirecting traffic to compromised machines. Setting static routes within the system (typically a single default route to a trusted router) protects the system from incorrect routes. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra to 0 disables the system's ability to accept IPv6 router advertisements.

rules.title: Firewalld is installed
rules.explanation: firewalld is a high-level firewall-rule management utility. It does not filter packets directly and relies on the nftables subsystem in the Linux kernel.
rules.impact: firewalld is a dynamic, user-friendly firewall manager that can protect against threats originating from the corporate network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host.

rules.title: Nftables is not used
rules.explanation: On AKS Optimized Azure Linux, iptables is recommended for the host-based firewall; nftables must not be active.
rules.impact: Verifying that the internal mechanism is correctly configured ensures critical firewall functionality.
rules.scope: nftables package, nftables.service, nft list ruleset output

rules.title: Firewalld is not used
rules.explanation: firewalld conflicts with iptables on minimal Azure Linux images for AKS nodes.
rules.impact: firewalld.service must be active to apply rules configured through FirewallD. firewalld.service must be enabled to start automatically after a system reboot.

rules.title: Access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and files ending in .conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory contain configuration specifications for sshd.
rules.impact: sshd configuration specifications must be protected against unauthorized modification by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Access to SSH host private key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH private key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In this authentication method, possession of the private key is proof of identity.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the SSH host private key file, the host may be compromised.
rules.scope: SSH private key file permission parameters in /etc/ssh/

rules.title: Access to SSH host public key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.
rules.scope: SSH public key file permission parameters in /etc/ssh/

rules.title: Sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: Available options to restrict users and groups that can access the system via SSH.
rules.impact: Restricting which users can remotely access the system via SSH helps ensure that only authorized users obtain access.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, DenyGroups

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies the file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Displaying a warning message before a user logs in can assist in the prosecution of computer system trespassers.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: Banner, and contents of the specified file

rules.title: Sshd ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: This variable restricts the ciphers that SSH may use during communication.
rules.impact: Weak ciphers used for authentication in a cryptographic module cannot provide confidentiality or integrity, and system data may be compromised.

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeout.
rules.impact: To prevent resource exhaustion, appropriate values should be set for both ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax. If connections are allowed to remain open indefinitely, this can potentially be used as a DDoS attack, or simple resource exhaustion may occur on unreliable networks.

rules.title: Sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding parameter disables all forwarding features, including X11, ssh-agent, TCP, and StreamLocal.
rules.impact: X11 forwarding is disabled unless there is an operational need to use X11 applications directly. Leaving port forwarding enabled may expose the organization to security risks and backdoor creation.

rules.title: Sshd GSSAPI authentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter specifies whether GSSAPI-based user authentication is permitted.
rules.impact: Allowing GSSAPI authentication over SSH exposes the system to GSSAPI from remote hosts and should be disabled to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows an authorized user to run a command as the superuser or another user in accordance with the security policy.
rules.impact: Security policy defines which privileges, if any, a user has to run sudo.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal.
rules.impact: Attackers can use sudo to launch a malicious program that creates a background process that remains even after the main program terminates.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/*: Defaults use_pty

rules.title: The sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: The Defaults logfile setting specifies the sudo log file path.
rules.impact: Defining a dedicated log file for sudo simplifies auditing of sudo commands and creating auditd rules for sudo.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/*: Defaults logfile

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users are required to enter a password to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication, users may gain access to resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to extend functionality, it is critical that the user reauthenticates.
rules.scope: Settings in files /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/*: tag NOPASSWD

rules.title: Sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: Key exchange is any cryptographic method by which two parties exchange cryptographic keys, enabling use of a cryptographic algorithm. If the sender and receiver wish to exchange encrypted messages, each must be equipped to encrypt outgoing messages and decrypt incoming messages. Notes: • Kex algorithms have higher priority the earlier they appear in the list • Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved key-exchange algorithms • ensure that the key-exchange algorithms in use comply with site policy • The only key-exchange algorithms currently approved under FIPS 140 are: o ecdh-sha2-nistp256 o ecdh-sha2-nistp384 o ecdh-sha2-nistp521 o diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 o diffie-hellman-group16-sha512 o diffie-hellman-group18-sha512 o diffie-hellman-group14-sha256
rules.impact: Key exchange methods that are considered weak should be removed. A key exchange method may be weak because too few bits are used or the hashing algorithm is considered too weak. Using weak algorithms can expose connections to man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: Sudo timestamp_timeout is configured
rules.explanation: sudo caches used credentials for 5 minutes by default.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged access as another user.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. Typically, any user can execute the su command.
rules.impact: Restricting the use of su and using sudo instead provides system administrators better control over user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/pam.d/su: pam_wheel.so, and group in /etc/group

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents should be sent to the remote user before authentication is allowed. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message before a user logs on normally can help hold attackers accountable on a computer system.

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: Note: To clarify: the two settings described below apply only to idle connections from a protocol perspective and are not intended to check whether a user is active. An idle user does not mean an idle connection. SSH does not, and never has, provided a capability to intentionally disconnect idle users. In SSH versions prior to 8.2p1 there was a bug that caused these values to behave in a way that was abused to disconnect idle users. That bug was fixed in version 8.2p1, and therefore can no longer be abused to disconnect idle users. The two options ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control the SSH session timeout. Taken directly from man 5 sshd_config: • ClientAliveInterval Sets a timeout interval in seconds after which, if no data has been received from the client, sshd(8) will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response from the client. The default is 0, indicating that these messages will not be sent to the client. • ClientAliveCountMax Sets the number of client alive messages that may be sent without sshd(8) receiving any messages from the client. If this threshold is reached while sending client alive messages, sshd will disconnect the client, terminating the session. It is important to note that the use of client alive messages is very different from TCPKeepAlive. Client alive messages are sent over the encrypted channel and therefore cannot be spoofed. The TCP Keepalive option enabled by TCPKeepAlive can be spoofed. The client alive mechanism is useful when the client or server depends on knowing when a connection has become unresponsive. The default is 3. If ClientAliveInterval is set to 15 and ClientAliveCountMax is left at the default, unresponsive SSH clients will be disconnected after approximately 45 seconds. Setting ClientAliveCountMax to zero disables connection termination.
rules.impact: To prevent resource exhaustion, appropriate values must be set for both ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax. In particular, reviewing the source code shows that ClientAliveCountMax must be greater than zero for SSH to disconnect idle connections. If connections are allowed to remain open indefinitely, this can potentially be used as a DDoS attack or simple resource exhaustion on untrusted networks. Page 245 For internal use only – general information. In the example given here, the timeout is 45 seconds. Review your site policy regarding network timeouts and apply it accordingly.

rules.title: Sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted.
rules.impact: Although .rhosts files are ineffective if support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: Sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH.

rules.title: Sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication on the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more open unauthenticated connections may exist. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a small value for the LoginGraceTime parameter will minimize the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It will also limit the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections. The recommended value is 60 seconds (1 minute), but set this value in accordance with site policy.

rules.title: Sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: SSH provides several logging levels with different degrees of verbosity. DEBUG options are specifically not recommended except solely for debugging SSH communications. These levels provide so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information and may violate user privacy.
rules.impact: INFO is the baseline level at which only SSH user login activity is recorded. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logout record can exclude users who have disconnected, which helps narrow the field. VERBOSE indicates that login and logout activity will be recorded, as well as the key fingerprint for any SSH key used to log in. This information is important for SSH key management, especially in legacy environments.

rules.title: Sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts allowed for a single connection. When the number of failed login attempts reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the failed login attempts will be written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting a small value for MaxAuthTries will minimize the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. The recommended value is 4, but set this number according to site policy.

rules.title: Sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxStartups parameter specifies the maximum number of concurrent unauthenticated connections to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service due to a large number of pending authentication connection attempts, use the MaxStartups rate-limiting feature to protect sshd login availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxSessions parameter specifies the maximum number of open sessions allowed for this connection.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service due to a large number of concurrent sessions, use the MaxSessions rate-limiting feature to protect sshd login availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits login to accounts with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote access to accounts with empty passwords reduces the likelihood of unauthorized system access.

rules.title: Sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user may log in via SSH. The default is prohibit-password.
rules.impact: Disallowing root logon over SSH requires system administrators to authenticate using their individual accounts and then elevate to root. This provides non-repudiation and a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.

rules.title: Sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to provide environment options to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path that causes SSH to execute Trojan programs).

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this enables PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM option is set to "yes", PAM correctly handles account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at login, or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy. The real (not effective) user ID of the calling user is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.
rules.impact: sudo supports a plugin architecture for security policy and I/O logging. Third parties can develop and distribute their own policy and I/O logging plugins to work seamlessly with the sudo interface. The default security policy is sudoers, which is configured via the /etc/sudoers file and any entries in /etc/sudoers.d. The security policy determines what privileges (if any) a user has to run sudo. The policy may require users to authenticate with a password or another authentication mechanism. If authentication is required, sudo will terminate if the user password is not entered within a configurable timeout. This restriction is policy-dependent.

rules.title: Re-authentication is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: The Defaults !authenticate directive in sudoers disables re-authentication for sudo.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to extend functionality, it is critical that the user reauthenticates.

rules.title: The sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: sudo caches used credentials for 5 minutes by default. This is done for ease of use when multiple administrative tasks must be performed. The timeout can be changed in accordance with local security policy.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged access as another user.

rules.title: Password creation requirements are configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module checks password strength. It performs checks such as verifying that the password is not a dictionary word, has a specified length, contains a mix of character types (for example, alphabetic, numeric, and so on), and similar. The following are the pam_pwquality.so parameter definitions. The following parameters are set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf: Password length: • minlen = 14 — the password must consist of 14 or more characters. Password complexity: • minclass = 4 — the minimum number of character classes required for the new password (digits, uppercase, lowercase, and so on) -OR- • dcredit = -1 — require at least one digit • ucredit = -1 — require at least one uppercase character • ocredit = -1 — require at least one special character • lcredit = -1 — require at least one lowercase character. The following is set in /etc/pam.d/system-password and /etc/pam.d/system-auth: • try_first_pass — retrieve the password from the previous stacked PAM module. If it is not available, prompt the user for a password. • retry=3 — allow 3 attempts before returning an error. The settings shown above are one possible policy. Change these values to match your organization's password policy. Notes: • Settings in /etc/security/pwquality.conf must use spaces around the = character. Page 278 For internal use only — common parameters • Additional module parameters can be set in /etc/pam.d/system-password and /etc/pam.d/system-auth.
rules.impact: Strong passwords and a limited number of attempts before account lockout protect systems from brute-force compromise.

rules.title: Lockout for failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: Lock users after n consecutive failed logon attempts. • Deny=<n> — the number of attempts before the account is locked. • unlock_time=<n> — the time in seconds before the account is unlocked. Note: The maximum configurable value for unlock_time is 604800.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks against your systems.

rules.title: The password hashing algorithm is SHA-512
rules.explanation: The following commands change password encryption from md5 to sha512 (a much stronger hashing algorithm). All existing accounts will need to change their password to update stored hashes to the new algorithm. Notes: • These changes apply only to accounts configured on the local system. • Additional module options may be set; the recommendations apply only to those listed here.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 algorithm provides much stronger hashing than MD5, thereby providing additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine passwords.

rules.title: Password reuse is restricted
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be checked to ensure that users are not reusing recent passwords.
rules.impact: Forcing users not to reuse their previous 5 passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker will be able to guess the password.

rules.title: The password expiration is 365 days or less
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows the administrator to force passwords to expire once they reach a certain age. It is recommended to set PASS_MAX_DAYS to a value less than or equal to 365 days.
rules.impact: The window of opportunity for an attacker to use compromised credentials or to successfully compromise credentials via an online brute-force attack is limited by the password lifetime. Therefore, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity.

rules.title: The minimum number of days between password changes is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days has passed since the user last changed their password. It is recommended that PASS_MIN_DAYS be set to 1 or more days.
rules.impact: By limiting the frequency of password changes, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to bypass password reuse controls.

rules.title: The password expiration warning is 7 days or more
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows the administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days. It is recommended to set PASS_WARN_AGE to 7 or more days.
rules.impact: Advance warning of password expiration gives users time to think of a secure password. Users caught by surprise may choose a simple password or write it down where it can be discovered.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is 30 days or less
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a defined period of time can be automatically disabled. It is recommended to disable accounts that have been inactive for 30 days after password expiration.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a system security threat because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: The last password change date for all users is already in the past
rules.explanation: All users must have a password change date in the past.
rules.impact: If a user's recorded password change date is in the future, they may bypass the configured password expiration.

rules.title: System accounts are secured
rules.explanation: Most distributions include a number of accounts used to manage applications that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that accounts that are not used by regular users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell. By default, most distributions set an invalid string in the password field for these accounts, but it is also recommended that the shell field in the password file be set to the nologin shell. This prevents potential use of the account to run any commands. Page 300 For internal use only – Overview

rules.title: The default group for the root account has GID 0
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root account belongs to. This affects access rights to files created by the root account.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent unprivileged users from accidentally accessing files owned by root.

rules.title: The default user umask is 027 or more restrictive
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine access permissions for newly created directories and files. On Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). umask changes the Linux default permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. The mask is not simply subtracted; it is processed bitwise. Bits set in the umask are cleared in the resulting file mode. umask can be set with octal or symbolic values: • Octal (numeric) value — represented by three or four digits, e.g. umask 0027 or umask 027. If a four-digit mask is used, the first digit is ignored. The remaining three digits affect the resulting permissions for user, group, and world/other respectively. • Symbolic value — represented by a comma-separated list for user u, group g, and world/other o. The listed permissions are not masked by umask. For example, a mask set with umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is the symbolic equivalent of octal mask 027. This mask will set a newly created directory to file mode drwxr-x--- and a newly created file to file mode rw-r-----. The default mask can be configured using the pam_umask module or in a system-wide shell configuration file. A user creating directories or files may at their discretion change permissions with the chmod command or select a different default umask by adding a umask command to a user shell configuration file (.bash_profile or .bashrc) in their home directory. Setting the default umask: • pam_umask module: o will set umask according to the system default in /etc/login.defs and user settings, addressing the problem of different umask settings for different shells, display managers, remote sessions, and so on. o The umask=<mask> value in /etc/login.defs is interpreted as octal. o Setting USERGROUPS_ENAB to yes in /etc/login.defs (the default): ▪ will set the umask group bits the same as the owner bits (examples: 022 -> 002, 077 -> 007) for non-root users if the uid is the same as the gid and the username is the same as <primary group name>. Page 305 Internal use only — common ▪ userdel will remove the user's group if it has no remaining members, and useradd will by default create a group named after the user. • System-wide shell configuration file: o /etc/profile — used to set system-wide environment variables in user shells. Sometimes the variables are the same as in .bash_profile; however, this file is used to set the initial PATH or PS1 for all system shell users. It is executed only for interactive login shells or shells invoked with the --login option. o /etc/profile.d — /etc/profile will execute scripts from /etc/profile.d/*.sh. It is recommended to place your configuration in a shell script under /etc/profile.d to set your own system-wide environment variables. o /etc/bashrc — the system-wide version of .bashrc. In Fedora-derived distributions, etc/bashrc also invokes /etc/profile.d/*.sh if the shell is not a login shell, but redirects output to /dev/null if it is non-interactive. Executed only for interactive shells or if BASH_ENV is set to /etc/bashrc. User shell configuration files: • ~/.bash_profile — executed to configure the shell before the initial command prompt. Read only by login shells. • ~/.bashrc — executed for interactive shells. Read only by an interactive non-login shell.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask value ensures that users make a conscious choice about file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog software is recommended in environments where Journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transport (that is, TCP), the ability to log in database formats, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: After installing the rsyslog package, ensure that the service is enabled.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not allowed to start at boot, the system will not record logging events.

rules.title: Default rsyslog file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: RSyslog will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. This parameter determines which permissions will be applied to newly created files.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions to enable archiving and protection of sensitive data.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive remote logs
rules.explanation: Receiving remote logs via imtcp/imudp in rsyslog is not required on AKS worker nodes.
rules.impact: If a client is configured to receive data, thereby turning it into a server, the client system operates outside its operational boundaries.

rules.title: Access to all log files is configured
rules.explanation: Log files contain information from many local system services or, in the case of a centralized log server, also logs from other systems. Log files are typically located in /var/log/, although an application can be configured to store logs elsewhere. If your application stores logs in another location, be sure to run the same test at that location.
rules.impact: It is important that log files have correct permissions to ensure sensitive data is protected and that only appropriate users/groups have access to them.

rules.title: Logrotate is configured
rules.explanation: The system includes the ability to rotate log files regularly to avoid filling the system with logs or allowing logs to grow unmanageably large. The /etc/logrotate.d/syslog file is the configuration file used to rotate log files created by syslog or rsyslog.
rules.impact: By keeping log files smaller and more manageable, the system administrator can easily archive these files to another system and spend less time reviewing excessively large log files.

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user-account information used by many system utilities, so it must be readable for those utilities to function.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/passwd from unauthorized write access.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/passwd file

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/passwd- from unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/passwd- file

rules.title: Access to /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains the list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users, but must remain readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/group file

rules.title: Access to /etc/group- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group- file contains a backup list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/group- from unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/group- file

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/shadow file

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow- file is used to store backup user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/shadow- from unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/shadow- file

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/gshadow file

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow- file is used to store backup group information that is critical to the security of these accounts.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/gshadow- from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file containing the full paths of valid login shells.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/shells from unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Access permission settings for the /etc/shells file

rules.title: Access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/security/opasswd and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old store users' previous passwords if pam_unix or pam_pwhistory is used on the system.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/security/opasswd from unauthorized access.
rules.scope: Access permission parameters for the /etc/security/opasswd file

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are protected
rules.explanation: World-writable files are the least secure.
rules.impact: Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World-writable files may also indicate a poorly written script or program that could potentially cause a more serious compromise of system integrity.
rules.scope: Permission parameters for all files and directories on the system

rules.title: There are no unowned or ungrouped objects
rules.explanation: Files and directories without an owner or group may indicate compromise or a container runtime failure.
rules.impact: A new user or group assigned the user ID or group ID of a deleted user may ultimately become the owner of the deleted user or group's files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts may use shadowed passwords.
rules.impact: The /etc/passwd file also contains information such as user and group IDs used by many system programs. Therefore, /etc/passwd must remain world-readable.
rules.scope: Parameters in the second column of /etc/passwd

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field means anyone can log on as that user without entering a password.
rules.impact: All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent use of the account by an unauthorized user.
rules.scope: Parameters in the second column of /etc/shadow

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group rights are not managed properly.
rules.impact: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group rights are not managed properly.
rules.scope: Parameters: GID in /etc/passwd and group existence in /etc/group

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access controls.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and proper access protection measures.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: Users must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Groups must be assigned unique names for accountability and proper access protection measures.
rules.impact: Groups must be assigned unique names for accountability and proper access protection measures.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: A user's home directory is space defined for a specific user to set local environment variables and store personal files. Although a system administrator can set secure permissions on user home directories, users can easily reverse them. Users may be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory, or with a home directory that does not actually exist.
rules.impact: Because the user is responsible for files stored in the user's home directory, the user should own that directory. Group-writable or world-writable user home directories may allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges. If a user's home directory does not exist or is not assigned, the user will be placed in "/" and will be unable to write any files or set local environment variables.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dotfiles is configured
rules.explanation: User configuration files with excessive or incorrect permissions may allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.
rules.impact: User configuration files with excessive or incorrect permissions may allow attackers to steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.
rules.scope: Permission parameters for "dot files" (.bashrc, .profile, and others) in user home directories
